claims.text: A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ (component state migrations guide) and it covers the callback contract for state migrations.
The pulumi/examples repository contains the directory aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration, an AWSX VPC state migration example with three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code.
Pulumi components let you turn a group of resources into a reusable building block that users consume through inputs and outputs without needing to understand every resource inside.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
Pulumi has a new component state migrations feature that lets component authors ship the upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Component authors can change a component's internal design and include the state migration in the same release.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
The AWSX VPC example follows a network through three versions: v1 (legacy), v2 (modern AWSX), and v3 (plain AWS), each building on the infrastructure already running.
The v1 of the AWSX VPC example uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component.
In the v1 AWSX VPC example, the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
In the v1 AWSX VPC example, a security group sits outside the VPC component and refers to the VPC.
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading from the legacy AWSX VPC component could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
An AWS EC2 security group refers to its VPC by ID, so a new VPC means the security group is replaced too (changing a security group's VpcId requires replacement).
The AWSX VPC state-migration example does not create a database.
Changes to a network used by a production database can cause downtime or require more resource replacements.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data; without a backup or data migration, deleting the old database could mean losing that data.
The v2 of the AWSX VPC example upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The v3 of the AWSX VPC example removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`, with Pulumi still managing them.
Across all three versions of the AWSX VPC example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.
In the resource trees for the AWSX VPC example, `awsx:` entries are component records and `aws:` entries represent the AWS resources that stay in place; the security group is outside the VPC tree.
The legacy AWSX VPC component uses resource type tokens `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc`, `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet`, and `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway`, while the modern AWSX VPC component uses `awsx:ec2:Vpc`.

In the resource trees, v1 places the subnet and internet gateway under separate `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet` and `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway` components, v2 places the subnet and internet gateway directly under the `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` beneath `awsx:ec2:Vpc`, and v3 has the `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` as the top-level record.
Pulumi's state records both the physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN.
Managed resources in Pulumi state also have an ID from the cloud provider, such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components.
Modern AWSX removes the subnet and internet gateway wrapper components and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` when moving from legacy to modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.

Aliases alone are insufficient for the legacy-to-modern AWSX upgrade because it also needs to remove component wrappers and transfer references to the resources that replace them; a state migration describes that whole change together.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/aliases/ and another at /docs/iac/concepts/components/.
A component registers a state migration by passing an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option.
`migrateClassicVpc` comes from the example's migration file at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
The alias lets Pulumi find the old component; the state migration callback then receives the old component's saved state, followed by the state of its children.
In the example, the migration callback copies the saved records, changes their names and parents to match modern AWSX, and returns `newState` and `successors`.
The `newState` value returned by a state migration callback is the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children.
The `successors` value returned by a state migration callback is a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place.
In the example, the migration callback is safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, it does nothing.
In the example, the migration callback raises an error on an unexpected component type instead of guessing how to migrate it.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields, and moves the subnet under the managed VPC.
The two subnet entries in `successors` tell the Pulumi engine that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record.
Pulumi uses `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
The VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference to the VPC connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.

The v3 of the example declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`; the migration changes who defines those resources in the program and configuration can be adjusted in a separate update.
The modern AWSX VPC component does not support some subnet or routing layouts users may need.

The second migration (v3/migration.ts in the example) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it.
The second migration's code is at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v3/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
In the v3 example, the VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types (legacy and modern AWSX) and both migration callbacks.
When a component registers multiple state migration callbacks, Pulumi runs the callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version using the chained migrations.
A stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component lets its users skip versions without having to edit stack state by hand.
After a state migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In the AWSX VPC example, keeping resource IDs does not mean an empty preview: the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
To try the AWSX VPC example, start with `v1` and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.

Before each upgrade in the AWSX VPC example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.

When a component author registers the migration inside the component implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; when they upgrade the component and run Pulumi, it runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without knowing which resources moved or how saved state changed.
A state migration written and tested once by the component author is delivered to every team using the component with the new version.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the resource option documented on the state migrations page) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks must be idempotent.
A Pulumi state migration callback must return no result when the resource's state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing any provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi option reference at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the state migration callback API.

Component state migration callback state entries use the checkpoint resource format documented in the Pulumi developer docs deployment schema (pulumi-resource-state), which includes fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
A Pulumi component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The Pulumi restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (with update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
